prompt: Coleta writes its file at 23:30 and SAP loads it at 02:00. Which kind of coupling does this file transfer leave out?
hint: Ask what would happen if SAP were down at 23:30.

choices.text: Coupling in format
choices.why: Both sides still have to agree on the layout: which columns hold the litres, what the trailer says.

choices.text: Coupling in location, since both sides use one agreed directory
choices.why: The directory is a location both sides know, so this coupling stays.

choices.text: Coupling in time
choices.why: Right: neither side has to be running when the other is; the file waits in the directory.

choices.text: Coupling to the other side's internal tables
choices.why: That is the shared database's coupling; a file carries a layout both sides agreed, not anybody's tables.

prompt: Match each description to the integration style it belongs to.
hint: Format, time and location: which one is tight, which one is loose.

pairs.left: The receiver depends on what the other side's tables mean
Both sides must be up at the same moment
The sender does not know who receives
Written now and read hours later

prompt: Joana's map has 110 integrations, and the ESB carries 70 of them. How many go point to point, outside the ESB?
hint: A subtraction.

prompt: Put the steps of a safe file integration in order, from the writer to the reader and back.
hint: The file has to exist whole before anybody can check it.
items: Write the file under a temporary name, with a header and a trailer
Rename it when the last line is written
Check the shape and compare the lines with the trailer's totals
Refuse it if its day and sequence were already loaded
Send an acknowledgement or a reject file back
trap: Loading before checking the totals posts goods receipts from a file that might be short of a line.

prompt: A Coleta file's trailer says 6 farms and 11237 litres. The farm lines in the file add up to 5 farms and 10277 litres. How many litres are missing?
hint: The trailer is what the writer promised; the lines are what arrived.

prompt: The writer creates the file under a temporary name and ___ it once the last line is down, so that a reader polling the directory never sees half a file.
hint: On one file system this operation is atomic.

prompt: For four nights in March 2025 no Coleta file arrived, and the 02:00 load finished without an error each night. Which control would have raised it on the first night?
hint: There was no file for any check to read.

choices.text: A trailer carrying the number of farm lines and the litres
choices.why: A trailer is checked when a file arrives; on those nights there was no file to check.

choices.text: Writing under a .tmp name and renaming
choices.why: That stops a half-written file being read; it does nothing about a file that was never written.

choices.text: Refusing a day and sequence already loaded
choices.why: That protects against a second load of the same file, not against the absence of one.

choices.text: An alarm at 01:30 when the day's file has not arrived
choices.why: Yes: absence is the failure a file hides, so the alarm is on the file that did not come.

prompt: An operator re-runs the night's load after a timeout, not knowing that it had already finished. The file is whole. What stops 1,870 farms being paid for that day's milk twice?
hint: The trailer's totals agree on both runs.

choices.text: The loader recording each file it loaded and refusing a repeat
choices.why: Right: a second run of a loader that remembers day and sequence changes nothing.

choices.text: The control totals in the trailer
choices.why: The file is whole, so its totals agree on the first run and on the second.

choices.text: The acknowledgement file sent back to Coleta after the load
choices.why: The acknowledgement tells Coleta what happened; it does not stop SAP posting the same lines again.

choices.text: The rename from the temporary name
choices.why: The rename happened once, on Coleta's side, long before either load ran.

prompt: Coleta starts marking a suspended farm with a new status value instead of deleting its row. Rota still reads Coleta's farm table directly. What happens?
hint: The shape of the table did not change.

choices.text: Rota's query fails that night, as it did in 2023
choices.why: In 2023 a column was split, so the query broke. Here no column changed, so nothing breaks.

choices.text: Trucks keep going to farms that stopped supplying
choices.why: Yes: a change of meaning with no change of shape is the quiet failure of reading somebody's table.

choices.text: Rota is unaffected, because it reads just the farm columns it needs
choices.why: The columns Rota reads are fine; what changed is what a row in them means.

choices.text: Coleta's screens slow down for the lab technicians
choices.why: Load on the owner's database is a real cost of direct reads, but this change does not add any.

prompt: Compared with querying another system's tables on a schedule, what does change data capture improve? Choose all that apply.
hint: It reads the database's log of changes.

choices.text: No load on the tables the application is using
choices.why: Yes: the log is written anyway, and reading it scans no table.

choices.text: Deletes arrive, in commit order
choices.why: Yes: a query looking for new rows never sees a row that has gone.

choices.text: The table's columns stop being the contract
choices.why: A CDC event is a row before and after; split a column and the events change shape too.

choices.text: No waiting for the next poll
choices.why: Yes: each change is published as it is committed.

prompt: A finance workbook reads SAP ECC's material document tables directly, and after the move to S/4HANA it still opens without errors. Why is it still a line on the migration plan?
hint: Where does the data it reads now come from?

choices.text: S/4HANA refuses connections from spreadsheets
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says so; the workbook opens, which is the point of the question.

choices.text: It needs a read replica first, to take the load off SAP
choices.why: A replica answers the load, the one cost that is not about the migration.

choices.text: It now reads compatibility views that SAP keeps for as long as SAP decides
choices.why: Right: the data moved to MATDOC, and the old names survive as views on SAP's terms.

choices.text: Its totals double, because MATDOC repeats every item
choices.why: The views return the documents once; the risk is who controls them, not double counting.

prompt: The stock check goes from the portal through the ESB to SAP, and each of the three is available 99.5% of the time. Assuming they fail independently, what is the chain's availability, in percent, to one decimal place?
hint: Multiply the three.

prompt: With the chain's availability at 98.507%, about how many hours of a 30-day month (720 hours) is the stock check unavailable? Give one decimal place.
hint: The unavailable share is 100% minus the availability.

prompt: The portal waits 10 seconds for the ESB and the ESB waits 60 seconds for SAP. What does that pair of settings produce when SAP takes 30 seconds?
hint: Who is still waiting at second 20?

choices.text: The bakery waits the full 60 seconds
choices.why: The bakery's wait ends with the portal's attempts, at 30 seconds in that incident.

choices.text: The ESB answers the portal before SAP does
choices.why: The ESB has no answer to give until SAP replies or its own 60 seconds run out.

choices.text: Work in SAP that nobody is waiting for
choices.why: Yes: the inner wait outlasts the outer one, so SAP finishes checks the portal already gave up on.

choices.text: The portal's retries wait until the first SAP check has finished
choices.why: Each retry starts a new call at once; that is how SAP ended up with three checks for one basket.

prompt: It is the closing week, and SAP is answering stock checks in 25 seconds. A bakery presses the checkout button. What does the lesson's design do?
hint: The answer was first built for Sunday nights.

choices.text: Retries quickly three times so the bakery is not kept waiting
choices.why: Quick retries into a slow system add load to it; that is what tripled SAP's checks in October.

choices.text: Raises the portal's timeout to 60 seconds
choices.why: Then the bakery waits a minute; the fix was shorter timeouts, shrinking towards SAP.

choices.text: Fails the checkout and asks the bakery to try again later
choices.why: That is the 212 failed checkouts of 2 October, turned into a policy.

choices.text: Shows the last stock figure with its time, and confirms later
choices.why: Right: the planned behaviour for a slow SAP is the Sunday one, used whenever the timeout runs out.

prompt: Which of these messages is an event rather than a command?
hint: Look at the tense, and at who decides what happens next.

choices.text: Create customer 30117 in Salesforce
choices.why: Imperative, aimed at one receiver: the sender has decided what Salesforce must do.

choices.text: Invoice 4711 was authorised
choices.why: Right: a fact in the past tense, for any number of receivers to act on as they choose.

choices.text: Send the certificate of batch 2210 to the supermarket chain
choices.why: An instruction to do one thing for one party is a command, whatever carries it.

choices.text: Recalculate the freight on order 4711
choices.why: It asks somebody to act; an event states what already happened and asks nothing.

prompt: Serra Alta issues about 1,400 invoices a weekday, and today each one is sent by call to three receivers. How many calls is that a day?
hint: One call per invoice per receiver.

prompt: Salesforce's consumer of the invoice topic stops for three hours. How does that failure show itself?
hint: The broker keeps the messages.

choices.text: As an error in SAP for each invoice published during those three hours
choices.why: SAP publishes to the broker and waits for nobody, so it sees no error at all.

choices.text: As three hours of invoices lost, to be re-sent from SAP
choices.why: The messages wait in the broker; nothing is lost and nothing is re-sent.

choices.text: As a lag: the oldest unconsumed message keeps getting older
choices.why: Yes: a stopped consumer produces no errors, which is why the alarm is on the age of the oldest message.

choices.text: As the portal and the EDI flow stopping too
choices.why: Each consumer reads the topic on its own; the other two never notice.

prompt: The invoice event carries only the invoice number, and each of the three consumers then calls SAP for the amount and the customer. What has that design brought back?
hint: When does SAP have to be up now?

choices.text: Coupling in time
choices.why: Right: SAP has to be up whenever a consumer processes an event, as if the consumers called it directly.

choices.text: SAP knowing who the three consumers are
choices.why: SAP still publishes to a topic; it answers calls without needing to know in advance who will make them.

choices.text: SAP waiting for each consumer before the next invoice
choices.why: Publishing still waits for nobody; the waiting is on the consumers' side.

choices.text: A contract covering every field of the invoice
choices.why: A thin event has fewer fields to promise; the full contract comes with carrying the state.

prompt: Match each Serra Alta integration to the style Joana decided for it.
hint: Who waits, how fresh, and how many consumers.

pairs.left: Coleta → SAP, the farms' daily litres
Portal B2B → SAP, stock at checkout
SAP → Rota, each plant's intake plan

right_distractors: a direct read of the other system's tables

prompt: Why does Joana keep Coleta → SAP as a file instead of moving it to events?
hint: Who waits for the litres, and for how long will Coleta exist?

choices.text: SAP cannot receive messages from a system on IBM i
choices.why: SAP takes messages from MQ, and IBM i can put them there; the reason is elsewhere.

choices.text: Nobody needs the litres before morning, and Coleta is being replaced
choices.why: Yes: nothing waits on it, and a new interface on IBM i would be code nobody maintains after 2028.

choices.text: Files are more reliable than events
choices.why: A file has its own failures, which is why it needs a trailer, a refusal of repeats and an alarm.

choices.text: The bank defines the format
choices.why: That is the CNAB file's reason; Coleta's layout is Serra Alta's own.

prompt: Supermarket chains ask for certificates of analysis by batch number. Why does Joana give them an API rather than publishing every certificate as an event?
hint: Who wants which certificates, and when?

choices.text: Documentum has no way to publish events
choices.why: The lesson does not argue from Documentum's features; it argues from who asks and when.

choices.text: Events are too small to carry a PDF
choices.why: Size is not the reason given; the demand is.

choices.text: A call costs less to operate than a broker
choices.why: Serra Alta already runs a broker; cost is not what decided this row.

choices.text: Few customers want them, for some batches, at moments nobody predicts
choices.why: Right: somebody waits, the document must be current, and sending all of them to everybody is traffic for nothing.

prompt: Rota reads Coleta's farm table directly and works today. Following the lesson, what should Joana do about it now? Choose all that apply.
hint: The map is a list of decisions, not of rebuilds.

choices.text: Write an owner for it on the map
choices.why: Yes: a style supplies no owner, and every row needs one.

choices.text: Rebuild it as an event this quarter
choices.why: A working row in another style is not automatically worth moving; the plan moves the four reading SAP.

choices.text: Tell Sebastião which columns Rota depends on
choices.why: Yes: then the next change to them is a conversation rather than routes planned by hand.

choices.text: Add an alarm for the night the plan is not produced
choices.why: Yes: the 2023 failure was noticed by dispatchers, not by any alarm.

prompt: A new system at the Lavras plant records each pallet of butter produced, about 300 a day. SAP's stock must show a pallet within minutes, nobody waits on the production line for SAP, and SAP stops every Sunday from 01:00 to 05:00. Which style fits?
hint: Fresh, nobody waiting, and a receiver that is sometimes down.

choices.text: A file written each night at 23:30
choices.why: Stock would be up to a day old, and the plant needs it within minutes.

choices.text: A call to SAP per pallet, retried until SAP answers
choices.why: Nobody is waiting for an answer, and on Sunday nights the retries would run for four hours.

choices.text: An event per pallet, held by the broker through Sunday
choices.why: Right: fresh in minutes, no waiting, and the broker keeps the Sunday pallets until SAP is back.

choices.text: SAP reading the new system's pallet table every five minutes
choices.why: That is the integration table again, with nobody watching its error rows and SAP's job polling for nothing.

prompt: For an event integration, the alarm is set on the ___ of the oldest unconsumed message, because a consumer that has stopped produces no errors.
hint: How long it has been waiting.

prompt: Joana's map shows 17 database links, 15 of them with no way to notice a failure. What does her plan for next year do with them?
hint: Which of them would break in the S/4HANA migration anyway?

choices.text: Moves all 17 to events, the style the table prefers
choices.why: The table decides new rows; for working ones, the cost of changing has to be weighed.

choices.text: Moves the four reading SAP; the rest get an owner and an alarm
choices.why: Yes: those four break in the migration anyway, and the others are decisions, not rebuilds.

choices.text: Leaves them as they are, since a working integration is best left alone
choices.why: Fifteen rows nobody watches are not working in any sense an owner would accept.

choices.text: Replaces them with calls, the best-watched style
choices.why: Calls are watched because they fail in front of somebody; that is no reason to add a time dependency.
